title: With Due Respect (Vol. 2) -- Ch. 7: Demystifying the Court
primary_topics: Chapter 7 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 2) -- CJP's July 4, 2010 Inquirer column on demystifying 'the most mysterious among major government agencies,' noting the Court's May 4, 2010 codification of its processes as 'The Internal Rules of the Supreme Court' (A.M. No. 10-4-20-SC)

How the Court sits en banc or in three five-member divisions (a division ruling being as final as an en banc one), with the most important cases reserved to the banc (constitutionality of a treaty/law/EO, death penalty, novel questions, reversals of jurisprudence, huge financial impact)

The settled but 'controversial' rule that the en banc does not exercise appellate jurisdiction over the divisions -- though, under the Court's all-embracing power to suspend its own Rules 'as it may decide to be just, fair and proper,' division judgments have at times still been elevated and reversed

The Court's caseload and machinery: roughly 6,000 new cases a year (vs. the US Court's ~10,000 petitions and ~100 accepted), about 30 cases raffled monthly to each justice, and the new 'Member-in-Charge' role under the Internal Rules, distinct from the eventual ponente
sub_topics: Why demystify: the midnight-CJ controversy briefly focused attention on the Court, yet it remains 'the most mysterious among major government agencies,' its processes unknown because, unlike trial courts, 'the public discovers a case only after a judgment is issued'

CJP's own remedy: his 'self-imposed duty' over his Supreme Court years to 'write a book each year to demystify the judicial processes'; now the Court itself did better, codifying its little-known processes in the Internal Rules (A.M. No. 10-4-20-SC, May 4, 2010)

The Rules' caveat: nothing in them limits the Court's constitutional and legal powers, and they may be 'amended, revised, deleted, suspended or dispensed with in particular cases' as the en banc 'may decide to be just, fair and proper'

En banc vs. division: the Court acts en banc (all members) or in three five-member divisions, and 'a decision rendered by any of the three divisions is deemed a decision of the Court itself,' as valid and final as an en banc judgment

Cases reserved to the banc (Section 3, Rule 2): those questioning the constitutionality of a treaty, law or executive order; imposing the death penalty; raising novel questions; reversing earlier jurisprudence; or carrying huge financial impact on business

'Not appealable to the banc': as a rule the banc does not review or modify division decisions, a division's denial of a motion to refer is 'final and not appealable,' and the banc may decline cognizance -- yet division judgments have at times been elevated and reversed under the power to suspend the Rules

Caseload: roughly 6,000 new cases a year, disposed of by minute resolutions, extended resolutions, or signed 'ponencias' -- against the US Supreme Court's ~10,000 petitions, of which it accepts about 100 for plenary review (always sitting en banc with nine members)

The raffle and the 'Member-in-Charge': about 30 cases are raffled monthly to each justice (atop 300-1,000 pending), yielding 1,200-1,500 full decisions a year; under the new Rules the justice raffled a case becomes the 'Member-in-Charge' who oversees and leads it but may or may not become ponente, and if the draft ponencia loses the vote, the majority appoints a new ponente (usually the main dissenter), converting the old draft into a dissent

stances.claim: The Court is 'the most mysterious among major government agencies' because the public learns of a case only after judgment -- a problem CJP addressed by writing a book a year, and which the Court itself eased by codifying its processes in the May 2010 Internal Rules.
stances.rhetorical_move: demystification framing: naming the opacity problem and the corrective (his books and the Internal Rules)

stances.claim: A division ruling is as final and binding as an en banc one, and the en banc 'does not exercise appellate jurisdiction over the divisions' -- yet under its all-embracing power to suspend the Rules 'as it may decide to be just, fair and proper,' the banc has at times still reviewed and reversed division judgments.
stances.rhetorical_move: rule-then-exception: stating the settled rule, then candidly noting how the Court's flexible power qualifies it

stances.claim: Despite a far heavier caseload than the US Court (about 6,000 new cases and 1,200-1,500 full decisions a year, vs. ~100 accepted in the US), the Philippine Court manages through the raffle system and the new 'Member-in-Charge' role, which separates case management from authorship of the eventual ponencia.
stances.rhetorical_move: comparative-workload framing plus mechanism: contextualizing the Court's burden and explaining the new internal division of labor

notable_anecdotes: A book a year: CJP recounts making it his 'self-imposed duty,' over his years on the Court, to write a book annually 'to demystify the judicial processes and to report to the public the Court's work for that year.'

6,000 vs. 10,000 -- but 100 accepted: he contrasts the Philippine Court's roughly 6,000 new cases and 1,200-1,500 full decisions a year with the US Court's ~10,000 petitions, of which only about 100 are accepted for plenary review.
30 cases a month: he reports that each justice is raffled about 30 new cases monthly atop a backlog of 300 to over 1,000 -- a vivid measure of the workload behind the robes.

Ponente becomes dissenter: under the new Rules, he explains, if a draft ponencia fails to win a majority, the would-be ponente's opinion 'may be converted into a dissenting opinion,' and the main dissenter writes the decision.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 7 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 2), CJP's July 4, 2010 Inquirer column, sets out to demystify 'the most mysterious among major government agencies' -- the Supreme Court, whose processes stay hidden because, unlike trial courts, 'the public discovers a case only after a judgment is issued.' He recalls making it his 'self-imposed duty' to write a book each year to explain the Court's work, and notes that the Court itself did better on May 4, 2010 by codifying its processes as 'The Internal Rules of the Supreme Court' (A.M. No. 10-4-20-SC) -- rules that, by their own caveat, cannot limit the Court's constitutional powers and may be 'amended, revised, deleted, suspended or dispensed with' as the en banc finds 'just, fair and proper.' He explains that the Court sits en banc or in three five-member divisions, that 'a decision rendered by any of the three divisions is deemed a decision of the Court itself,' and that the most important cases (constitutionality of a treaty, law or EO; the death penalty; novel questions; reversals of jurisprudence; huge financial impact) are reserved to the banc. He lays out the 'controversial but well settled' rule that the banc does not exercise appellate jurisdiction over the divisions -- a division's denial of a referral motion is 'final and not appealable' -- while candidly noting that the banc has at times still reviewed and reversed division judgments under its power to suspend the Rules. On workload, he contrasts the Court's roughly 6,000 new cases and 1,200-1,500 full decisions a year with the US Court's ~10,000 petitions and ~100 acceptances, and describes the raffle system (about 30 cases a month per justice) and the new 'Member-in-Charge' role, which oversees a case but may not become its ponente -- so that if a draft ponencia loses the vote, the main dissenter writes the decision and the old draft becomes a dissent.
